The same model, with the same weights, scores 62% in one agent harness and 33% in another.

@adithya...
items.content:
The same model, with the same weights, scores 62% in one agent harness and 33% in another.

@adithya_s_k and the @huggingface team just released the ultimate guide to multi-harness RL, and it's one of the most practical RL write-ups this year, and everything open!

The trick is simple. Don't touch the harness. Point it at a proxy instead of the model. The proxy speaks all four API formats coding agents use (OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic Messages, Gemini). It records the exact token ids and logprobs vLLM sampled, and you train on that. You don't change a single line of Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode.

Results:
🔹 Trained across 4 harnesses at once, LFM2.5-2.6B by @liquidai went from 42% to 54%
🔹 31% fewer tool calls, thanks to a small bonus for solving tasks in fewer steps
🔹 Training in OpenCode alone took OpenCode from 34% to 58%, but the multi-harness model improved everywhere

They also tried the shortcut everyone reaches for: fine-tune on 3,189 successful rollouts from Qwen3.8-27B. Imitation plateaued at 47.5%, below both RL runs. Copying a bigger model doesn't get you there. Practice does.

The best part is that everything is open: the capture proxy in OpenEnv, the trainer in TRL, the tasks, the SFT data, the training code and all seven trained models.
Agents will run in dozens of harnesses. 

Now open models can be trained for each of them, by anyone.

Read it here 👇
https://t.co/s2I8GI9SLS

Project Suncatcher has liftoff! ☀️🚀

Announced last year, this moonshot project explores if we can o...
items.content:
Project Suncatcher has liftoff! ☀️🚀

Announced last year, this moonshot project explores if we can one day host machine learning infrastructure in space. After years of research, we’ve just launched a prototype satellite, built in partnership with @planet, into orbit on @SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission.

This initial mission will gather data on how @Google TPUs handle the physical stress and extremes of spaceflight. Ultimately, these findings will help us explore how to potentially link multiple satellite constellations for scaled machine learning. By operating in low Earth orbit, these systems can tap into near-constant sunlight to generate up to 8x more solar power than on Earth.

items.title: Today we're unveiling Trillium Labs @trillium_labs, a new non-profit to foster the open science of f...
items.content:
Today we're unveiling Trillium Labs @trillium_labs, a new non-profit to foster the open science of frontier AI. We're building open post-training recipes and will expand into open infra to study RSI, reward-hacking, multi-agent systems, and whatever comes next.

We're built around the theory of change that you need more eyes to solve hard technical problems. We have faith in the scientific methods and communities that humanity has built, and worry that AI is becoming too closed to utilize them.

Trilliums are wildflowers that bloom briefly in the spring, before the forest canopies fill out. Though they are small, they lay the foundation for the cycles of growth and nourishment through the rest of the year. At Trillium Labs, the recipes will be the slow nutrients for the seasons and the model releases will be the blooms. Building an institution dedicated to this is needed because, much as nature’s trilliums are slow to expand and grow, the open-ecosystem needs time and dedicated resources to catch up.

I co-founded with with a long-time friend and collaborator Tom Zick (@thesezickbeats). We're hiring (full time + student collabs/interns), we're fundraising, and we're looking for compute. Please get in touch if you're interested in helping out. Offices based in the Bay Area and Cambridge MA, remote okay.

I’m in the Bay Area until for The Curve and COLM to connect with people who are interested. We’re thankful to have initial support from Halcyon Futures and Schmidt Sciences with more funding en route to enable our ambitions of scaling. Our advisors @Thom_Wolf, @HannaHajishirzi, @gneubig and @ctnzr have been instrumental to building the ecosystem that exists today, and I’m stoked to get to keep working with them.

items.title:
a few open source contributions from perplexity recently:

•pplx-decider-v1-27b: SoTA multimodal dec...
items.content:
a few open source contributions from perplexity recently:

•pplx-decider-v1-27b: SoTA multimodal decision model. 85.7% average across 11 benchmarks, ahead of Jev.
•pplx-embed-v2-context-9b-preview: SoTA contextual embeddings, best on ConTEB and turbopuffer context-bench.
•Lily: local inference engine for Apple silicon. rust plus custom metal kernels, no pytorch or mlx. 1.23x faster prefill and 1.35x faster decode than MLX-LM on an M5 Max
•PII-Tracer: 0.6B on-device PII classifier that decides when a hybrid compute task stays on your Mac. beats OpenAI’s Privacy Filter on all 5 public benchmarks. also released with the PII-TRACE benchmark: 13k conversations in 13 languages
•WANDR: benchmark for wide and deep research agents. 500 tasks needing 170k source-backed records
•Numbat: agent detection and response for laptops and workstations. 52 rules, single go binary for macOS, linux and windows
•Bumblebee: read-only supply chain scanner for dev machines. covers packages, MCP configs, and editor and browser extensions. 

a lot more open source contributions coming soon!

items.content:
It’s quite disturbing that Anthropic has been running a campaign to lobby the major faiths to adopt their own philosophical interpretation of AI, rather than taking input from them. 

I’ve been fortunate to spend time at the Vatican, and I’ve always asked for advice and guidance, answered the questions asked of me, and been grateful to them for their time and guidance. It’s insane to me Anthropic would actively impose their viewpoint to the extent of threatening to pull out of events that don’t precisely align.

It’s a moral arrogance and dogmatism that has characterised EA and Anthropic (certainly its leadership at least) for a very long time. I’m glad these stories are coming out and being exposed.

"The Argon model is a great example of how static benchmarks are really failing to assess the actual real-world performance of models."

"The big headline is that it's number one on text. But when you subset to experts, the model drops quite significantly. It goes from rank #1 to number #7."

"If you go to agentic tasks, the model is number #10. The top nine spots are all dominated by OpenAI and Anthropic. So the Argon model is just a solid number #3. A big improvement from the previous models they've released."
@arena

one of the most challenging tasks for frontier models is being able to extract thousands of values from extremely dense tables in documents.

our new Extract v2.5 agents are able to get 93%-96%+ on long-list extraction, including cells that fall in between pages. 

in contrast, astra gets ~30% accuracy over this benchmark. 

in these cases, frontier VLMs can stop early or miss repeated records. 

they also struggle to attribute each value back to the source. we are able to attribute every single extracted value back to the source.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Rep. Ro Khanna wants a worldwide pause on recursive self-improvement, written i...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Rep. Ro Khanna wants a worldwide pause on recursive self-improvement, written into a treaty with China.

• That's pillar one of five, and the one he calls the most likely path to losing control entirely. Asking AI to design its own safeguards is like asking the fox to guard the henhouse
• Pillar two: a global pause on superintelligence, defined as AI that exceeds human capability across all domains
• Pillar three: kill switches embedded in all advanced models, though he notes scientists disagree on how effective they'd be
• Pillar four: air-gapped sandbox testing of every model before release, American or Chinese
• Pillar five: verification tech and an inspection regime, invoking Reagan's trust but verify
• He's written directly to DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot asking if they'd join technical working groups and allow inspections, and to DNI Jay Clayton for intelligence assessments on loss of control

@theojaffee: "If you're going to have any kind of US-China AI treaty, you're going to need mutually trusted verification tech. And probably this should be more computational than reliant on humans. We don't want the US and China to have literal spies in each other's labs."

👉 https://t.co/MohU4A8Z...
items.content:
I keep going more niche with reverse engineered web-based versions of games

👉 https://t.co/MohU4A8Zel 👈

6 months ago I tried to reverse engineer Urban Terror

Urban Terror was kind of a Counter-Strike style mod on top of the Quake 3 Arena engine, I think @Erwin_AI got me to play this during COVID

Because it runs on Quake 3's engine like RTCW and Q3 itself, I thought I could just use ioquake3 and WASM to run it on web, then add a multiplayer server and it'd just work...

But no it didn't, I got stuck 6 months ago, it was buggy and wouldn't work, I kept trying and kinda got it to load but not really play

Today I tried it again with Opus 5.5 and again, I couldn't get it to work, giving up I did a last try with Fable 5.1 on high effort and it after awhile it did figure out the issue!

"The engine's struct was 4 bytes longer than what UT's bytecode expects, everything after that point (the entity count and the entity list) was read 4 bytes off"

It rewrote the bytecode and made it work!

So now we have another game preserved, running  100% the web via WASM, with a multiplayer server tied to it, so you can play with your friends 😊

Every model that comes out makes a bit more things possible and you can just keep trying old things that didn't work before

I see lots of people mod modern games now too which looks very cool too

Here I'm playing it with @marckohlbrugge a few minutes ago! Anyway you can play it with everyone else at https://t.co/MohU4A8Zel now :D

items.content:
.@AndrewYang on why AI growth won’t reach most Americans without UBI:

"AI is going to increase GDP and economic output very substantially. And right now GDP's at 84,000 a head. It's gonna pass 90 and then 100,000 a head, and then keep on going."

"The problem is that most Americans are not going to feel that in their own lives. They might see a number on a TV screen somewhere, but the money isn't gonna flow to them."

"I was saying $1,000 a month in 2020. Now that would be 1,250 a month, adjusted for inflation."

"That would be a game changer to millions of Americans. 1,250 a month would get the boot off their throat. And do I think that's enough? Do I think we should be doing more? I do. But I'd love to have that as a foundation or a floor."

"Right now we're in a bit of a bind where the work is going to be done by machines, and machines aren't gonna pay taxes, and then humans are gonna lose their jobs. And when we work, we do pay taxes."

"You're going to be in the worst of all worlds where the value is going someplace else. We're not gonna see taxable revenue, and then the tax base is going to shrink."

"That would be a game changer to millions of Americans. 1,250 a month would get the boot off their throat. And do I think that's enough? Do I think we should be doing more? I do. But I'd love to have that as a foundation or a floor."

"Right now we're in a bit of a bind where the work is going to be done by machines, and machines aren't gonna pay taxes, and then humans are gonna lose their jobs. And when we work, we do pay taxes."

"You're going to be in the worst of all worlds where the value is going someplace else. We're not gonna see taxable revenue, and then the tax base is going to shrink."

items.content:
.@AndrewYang on how to actually "tax AI, not humans":

"Dario Amodei said tax tokens. He suggested a 3% token tax. I'm gonna suggest that might be a little low, but his mechanism at least is great."

"You could tax the compute layer, and I think that's an effective proxy for AI."

"The other thing I'm going to suggest we're way behind the curve on, if we did this it would actually solve most of the problem, is we should have a value-added tax in the US which would, by the way, capture AI, capture compute."

"It's really straightforward for a multinational tech company to not pay meaningful income tax in America. You can just push all your income through Ireland. And you can't wriggle out of a value-added tax."

"We're still the richest market. We're the number one consumer market. Obviously, it's not a realistic threat for a US company to be like, 'We're not gonna sell there.'"

"A value-added tax at even half the European level, because our economy is so massive, our economy is at, let's call it 31 trillion or so, gets you maybe, like, 1.3 trillion, which would cover UBI almost in its totality."
@Fwd_Party

items.title: In my consumer research and in talking to people who build robots everyone wants a robot that looks ...
items.content:
In my consumer research and in talking to people who build robots everyone wants a robot that looks like them. 

Particularly in the hands. 

Then when building (or buying) reality sets in.

Four fingers does pretty well. Costs 1/5th less. Is easier for today’s AI to handle. Is more reliable (fewer parts to break).

At @mundanebot, which makes robots for dirty and dangerous jobs, I learned that two fingers can do about 40% of what a human hand can do. (This photo is of one of theirs).

Costs even less. 

My question is whether Elon will stick to the full Monty hand for Optimus even though fewer fingers would increase reliability and reduce cost?

Use the right tool for the job.

If I were Elon I would make it possible to use a variety of hands. That way he can satisfy customers no matter what their needs are for a lower price.

@SharpaRobotics’s hands, for instance, cost $50,000 each. 

Too expensive if two fingers does your job just great.

In other words @kokowaters_ is right. Robots will probably have non-human-looking hands in many cases.

Two-finger, or even four, don’t look as cool on social media, either, so I bet the best-selling robots will offer both.

Just look at how much work @sundayrobotics gets out of two fingers. It is why those companies with better AI will attract more buyers than the “sexy” bots that cost a lot more.

items.title: Arena CEO @ml_angelopoulos reveals why the "cheapest" AI model can stop looking cheap once you measu...
items.content:
Arena CEO @ml_angelopoulos reveals why the "cheapest" AI model can stop looking cheap once you measure cost per completed task instead of cost per token:

"Our goal is always to get deeper and deeper in people's real work."

"People are so fixated on cost per token. At Arena, we really believe that you need to be evaluating things on cost per task. On the Pareto frontier for agents, Claude's on the top, it's Sol, and the Gemini model is not quite Pareto frontier."

"It's telling you not just about the performance, but what's the ratio of how token hungry it is versus getting jobs done."

"If you look at token costs, the leaderboard looks completely different than it does if you look at task completion rates."
@arena

items.content:
If an honest CEO testifies before the Congress about AI:

-- Is it dangerous?

-- We don't know.

-- Is it not dangerous?

-- We don't know.

-- Can you make it not dangerous?

-- We don't know how.

-- Do you know how it works?

-- We know how to train it.

-- This wasn't my question.

-- We know how to run the inference cheaply.

-- This wasn't my question.

-- No, we don't.

-- Can you recognize when it will become dangerous?

-- Unlikely.

-- What do you need to be able to answer any of these questions?

-- Someone to stop us, but only if the Chinese stop too.

-- That's impossible. What else do you need?

-- A shitload of cash.

items.content:
Vals AI CEO @RayanKrishnan argues AI could create a new kind of inequality where the person with the smarter agent wins more negotiations, deals, and even lawsuits:

"If you talk to a lot of people at labs, they believe we will build intelligence too cheap to meter, and so a lot of these problems will be solved. But I go back and forth on this."

"If more of our work becomes delegated to personal assistants, then it becomes a matter of how well these agents can negotiate with one another. And you can get way better performance out of models by throwing more tokens and more capable intelligence at the task."

"If you have some juiced up Fable-level agent, and I just have a plebeian Sonnet agent that I'm using for free, you will win more negotiations against me. If you sue me, you will probably win. So there's a way in which intelligence will be a greater cause of inequality."

"On the whole, I'm still optimistic, because if anything, it will be a short period which will soon be eclipsed."
@ValsAI

items.title: I use AI to create pipelines that convert a book in HTML format hosted elsewhere into an interactive...
items.content:
I use AI to create pipelines that convert a book in HTML format hosted elsewhere into an interactive format used on ChapterPal.

Once a book is converted, there's a validation phase where I scroll through the entire converted book, spot conversion issues, and ask the AI to fix the converter.

Because third-party books can be in hundreds of different formats, each conversion pipeline results in its unique conversion artifacts.

When I scroll through a converted book, I easily see such artifacts.

But now we have models with vision and agents capable of opening webpages in a browser and scrolling through them to compare the source and the target, right?

Every time a new model or a new harness version is released, I ask the fucking PhD-level AGI/ASI to visually compare the source to the target and spot conversion artifacts. I don't give examples of what those artifacts might look like because they are all different for different sources.

The fucking PhD-level AGI/ASI is consistently useless. It can see that some words are missing, but everything about leaked HTML, math that is supposed to be in LaTeX but is in plain text, unescaped dollar signs, a list that is supposed to have bullets but doesn’t, and so on, it's all okay to the PhD-level AGI/ASI.

That's why I'm so annoyed hearing that those tin cans are sooo(...)oooo intelligent, beat the dumb ARC-AGI benchmarks like crazy, but cannot spot what looks "weird" in a target webpage compared to the source.

items.title: The UI designers of Codex, with each version update, move the "Commit and Push" option to a differen...
items.content:
The UI designers of Codex, with each version update, move the "Commit and Push" option to a different, less intuitive place. They don't realize that this option must be a huge green button in the top right corner.

Even more, this button must have a subbutton that sends the following prompt: "Pull the changes from Git by preserving the local changes. Then integrate the two and push to Git."

They don't understand how vibe coders work. We don't care about the branches, conflict resolution, and all that crap. If anything is broken, we just ask the AI to fix it, whatever the provenance of the bug.

We know that if merging of conflicts screws up, a fix is just one prompt away, and we make thousands of prompts daily.

Come on, @OpenAI, know your user already!

items.title: Vals AI CEO @RayanKrishnan argues "Claude is the salesman for Claude," because the model can eventua...
items.content:
Vals AI CEO @RayanKrishnan argues "Claude is the salesman for Claude," because the model can eventually find the inefficient parts of your life and insert itself into them:

"I was staying with a friend's parents, and the dad is a doctor in a hospital. Every month he spends 12 hours making the schedule for the hospital. I sat down with him for an afternoon, used Claude Code and made him a little web app, and this app has saved him 12 hours every month."

"I was asking this friend of mine at Anthropic, does this mean the biggest bottleneck will actually be behavior? He said, 'No, because over time, Claude will figure out the places where you're spending time in an inefficient way and suggest how to use itself for those tasks.'"

"Claude is the salesman for Claude. It's not going to be a human bottleneck. The model is itself the solution to a lot of these problems."
@ValsAI

Greatest Hits of Confidence

The “never,” “nobody,” and “it’s...
items.content:
@ashkaidev Here is its answer:

+++++

Greatest Hits of Confidence

The “never,” “nobody,” and “it’s over” edition

Robert, I searched the stored archive—no new X pulls. The index contains 4,445,587 posts. This was a broad search across it, not an exhaustive review of every record, so I can’t honestly claim to have found every badly aged post.

Here are the strongest receipts, with the less conclusive ones clearly separated.

1. Google quit the frontier-model race. Apparently nobody told Google.

August 27 — @OrganicGPT:
“At this point, I think it's safe to say that Google just gave up on building frontier models.”
From AI Community #1.
https://t.co/LgAo8tHD0U

September 30 — @GoogleDeepMind:
“Introducing Gemini 4 Argon – our new frontier model.”
From AI Organizations.
https://t.co/vZCUfz4ZGM

Shelf life: 34 days. A direct contradiction of “gave up.” The announcement was a limited trusted-tester rollout—not proof Google permanently won.

2. Nobody comes back to Cursor. Except the people coming back to Cursor.

March 9 — @gabriberton:
“Cursor is cooked. Any cursor user trying claude code does not go back.”
From Computer Vision.
https://t.co/rHPD9Vivo4

April 28 — @jianna_liu:
“switching back to cursor (from claude code) has been my saving grace the past week”
From AI Leaders #2.
https://t.co/6G127iaNHc

May 11 — @Jaytel:
“I'd have never guessed that I'm back to using Cursor”
From AI Community #6.
https://t.co/Bs0uGrwnOW

The word “any” did a lot of unnecessary work. This doesn’t settle market share; it directly defeats the no-return claim.

3. “AI cannot do math.” That is a very large conclusion from one test.

April 29 — @TheWhizzAI:
“Apple just proved AI cannot do math. Not advanced math. Grade school math.”
From AI Companies #2.
https://t.co/iMdwtGMSwj

May 24 — @haider1:
Reported that DeepMind’s AlphaProof Nexus solved nine formalized Erdős problems out of 353 attempted, including decades-old questions.
From AI Newsmakers.
https://t.co/vxSMaAkV5t

Verdict: overgeneralization, not a refutation of Apple’s specific experiment. The later archived report makes “AI cannot do math” look badly overstated. Different systems and tests aren’t interchangeable, and I haven’t independently reverified the paper.

4. “Wrappers aren’t businesses.” Revenue would like a word.

April 29 — @md_kadiwal:
“ai wrappers aren't businesses. they're bets that the api never improves. good luck with that.”
From AI Community #3.
https://t.co/PAaKt79EDN

September 28 — @higgsfield:
“To celebrate Higgsfield’s $1 Billion revenue run-rate, we’re resetting the subscription credits you’ve used this month.”
From AI Companies #2.
https://t.co/HOCovzj4KQ

An uncomfortable juxtaposition—not an airtight verdict. “Wrapper” is loosely defined, and company-reported run-rate is neither audited annual revenue nor profit. Still, dismissing the entire application layer as “not businesses” is a bold position.

Bonus tracks: people who corrected themselves

These deserve credit for updating, rather than being treated as stubbornly wrong.

5. The next TikTok became a goodbye.

March 24 — @JohnnotJon:
“The week Sora came out I really thought it might be the next TikTok. I thought wrong.”
From AI Leaders #1.
https://t.co/NTOho1IAS5

March 25 — @NBCNews:
Reported that OpenAI would shut down the Sora app, affecting Disney’s deal and planned investment.
From World News.
https://t.co/10hgC1q94x

An admitted miscall. I didn’t recover his original launch-week post, and “might” was never a guarantee.

6. The spectacular result had a recording problem.

May 5 — @facontidavide:
“I must apologize for over-promising in my last post,” while announcing a Cloudini release.
From AI Community #4.
https://t.co/MEwyK0U2bw

Later that day — @facontidavide:
“This aged terribly. Sorry, I got too excited and didn't realized my recording was wrong.”

He added that the improvements remained, but were less spectacular.
From AI Community #4.
https://t.co/FqtTV9qYaQ

A documented correction, not a recovered numerical before-and-after comparison. Refreshingly direct accountability.

The recurring mistake: turning a temporary lead, a narrow failure, or a personal preference into a universal law.

I left out unexpired predictions, satire, unsupported breach accusations, and “aged like milk” reactions where the original claim was missing. The two cleanest shareable pairs are Google quitting and nobody returning to Cursor.

items.title:
After trying the Reverse Osmosis (RO) filter and making V60 coffee with it, it tasted a bit flat

I ...
items.content:
After trying the Reverse Osmosis (RO) filter and making V60 coffee with it, it tasted a bit flat

I was kind of expecting that because even with the remineralizer installed (yes we have a remineralizer!) it only gets to 25 TDS, which is quite a low amount of mineral content for water

TDS means total dissolved solids, so like what's left after you remove all the water, essentially the mineral content

The plastic 6L water bottles we used before had a TDS of about 60

So I asked Claude what specialty coffee places do? They usually have an RO filter without any remineralizer. Then they use an industrial machine to remineralize it to the perfect level. That's why coffee of specialty coffee chains like @the_coffee (my fav) taste the same from Brazil to Japan. And their TDS level is high around 150

How can I do get my RO 25 up to 150 though? Claude suggested getting a mineral water coffee kit by Lotus Coffee, you get 4 drippers for Calcium, Magnesium, Potassium and Sodium, so I got it today and tried it. There's a specific amount of drops to add based on your current TDS

The TDS went up to 156 so at specialty coffee water level, and the V60 looked different and way more bubbly

And the flavor is great, it's not bitter, it's pure kind acidic like the Brazil beans we have should be

Adding these drops everytime might be annoying though, maybe I can mix them and make my own solution, or I can get a remineralizer for coffee that gets it to 150 TDS by itself after RO

Anyway I've become a coffee water snob now 🧔‍♂️ 🫣

"AI-Native LLM Security — Threats, Defense...
items.content:
From @PacktDataML — available at https://t.co/fmHgkRo26I

"AI-Native LLM Security — Threats, Defenses, and Best Practices for Building Safe and Trustworthy AI"

𝘽𝙤𝙤𝙠 𝘿𝙚𝙨𝙘𝙧𝙞𝙥𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣:
"Adversarial AI attacks present a unique set of security challenges, exploiting the very foundation of how AI learns. This book explores these threats in depth, equipping cybersecurity professionals with the tools needed to secure generative AI and LLM applications. Rather than skimming the surface of emerging risks, it focuses on practical strategies, industry standards, and recent research to build a robust defense framework.

Structured around actionable insights, the chapters introduce a secure-by-design methodology, integrating threat modeling and MLSecOps practices to fortify AI systems. You’ll discover how to leverage established taxonomies from OWASP, NIST, and MITRE to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities. Through real-world examples, the book highlights best practices for incorporating security controls into AI development life cycles, covering key areas such as CI/CD, MLOps, and open-access LLMs."

Amazon Summary:
“In Building AI-Powered Apps with Angular, you'll embark on an end-to-end journey to revolutionize web development with artificial intelligence. This hands-on guide shows you how to integrate cutting-edge AI capabilities, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) like Google Gemini and multimodal agents, directly into your Angular applications.

Starting with AI/ML fundamentals and an introduction to Google Gemini using Node.js, you’ll quickly progress to building sophisticated AI features within your Angular frontend. You’ll create dynamic content, design intelligent multi-turn chat interfaces, and harness multimodal AI to analyze and generate rich media such as images and videos.

The journey extends beyond the frontend. You’ll build robust backends with Angular Server-Side Rendering and Genkit, enabling seamless communication with AI models. 

You’ll also implement advanced search capabilities using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Firestore and learn how to deploy your AI-powered Angular app to the cloud.

By the end of the book, you'll have the skills to design, develop, and deploy innovative and intelligent Angular applications that leverage the full potential of AI”

Amazon Summary:

“In Building AI-Powered Apps with Angular, you'll embark on an end-to-end journey to revolutionize web development with artificial intelligence. This hands-on guide shows you how to integrate cutting-edge AI capabilities, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) like Google Gemini and multimodal agents, directly into your Angular applications.

Starting with AI/ML fundamentals and an introduction to Google Gemini using Node.js, you’ll quickly progress to building sophisticated AI features within your Angular frontend. You’ll create dynamic content, design intelligent multi-turn chat interfaces, and harness multimodal AI to analyze and generate rich media such as images and videos.

The journey extends beyond the frontend. You’ll build robust backends with Angular Server-Side Rendering and Genkit, enabling seamless communication with AI models.

You’ll also implement advanced search capabilities using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Firestore and learn how to deploy your AI-powered Angular app to the cloud.

By the end of the book, you'll have the skills to design, develop, and deploy innovative and intelligent Angular applications that leverage the full potential of AI”

.@AndrewYang reveals his path to an independent president by 2029, starting with just 3 senators holding the balance of power:

"What if I were to tell you that there could be three independent US senators in January of 2027? That could be a fulcrum."

"You could have a 49, 49 Senate, and then two in the middle or even three in the middle. And the three senators in the middle form a fulcrum of common sense."

"There are two US Senate candidates right now in Idaho and South Dakota that are running as independents, and the Democrats dropped out of the race in both of those states."

"You could have an independent president and cabinet and fulcrum in the Senate by beginning of 2029, if everything were to go incredibly well."

"50% of Americans say they're independent. Democrats and Republicans are both at around 25% each, and neither major party is going to solve any of the most pressing problems of our time."

"It's not gonna be the Democratic Party. It's not gonna be the Republican Party. So it's gotta be Americans rising up and saying, 'It's not left or right, but forward.'"
@Fwd_Party

.@AndrewYang: "I love Trump Accounts."

items.content:
.@AndrewYang: "I love Trump Accounts."

"I love Michael and Susan Dell. I love free money for infants, which is really what this boils down to."

"I think people who hate Trump accounts because they're called Trump accounts are really dumb. You can call it whatever you want. It's money for kids."

"There have been any number of Democrats, including Cory Booker, who've been trying to get something similar implemented in the form of a baby bond or something else."

"Michael Dell and Susan Dell, I believe, donated $6 billion of their own money. They did not have to."

"That $1,000 is gonna disappear very, very quickly if you actually have a kid."

"The hope is that someone takes the $1,000, and then they invest it, and it compounds, they add to it, and I love it. I love all of that."

"It's not like that amount of money's enough to reverse the bigger trends that are out there. But it's a great thing, and I love everyone who has made it happen."
@Fwd_Party
